statement: The system shall allow operations staff to set up the correlator for an observing run.
The system shall allow operations staff to verify that the correlator is behaving correctly.
The system shall keep the data flowing without interruption.
The system shall take the raw correlator output.
The system shall transform the raw correlator output into a usable form in real time.
The system shall hand the usable data off for storage and later analysis.
The system shall provide a clear view of system health.
The system shall provide a clear view of current observing status.
The system shall provide a clear view of the quality of the incoming data so that issues can be spotted quickly.
Where possible, the system shall detect faults on its own and recover automatically.
The system shall avoid losing data during an observation if it can be avoided.
The EVLA Correlator Operations System shall support configuration.
The EVLA Correlator Operations System shall support monitoring.
The EVLA Correlator Operations System shall handle the real-time data stream.
The EVLA Correlator Operations System shall provide health visibility.
The EVLA Correlator Operations System shall support fault recovery.
The system shall ensure that the data product gets through cleanly for downstream use.
The current process for monitoring the correlator is a hands-on operational process.
Staff monitor correlator status using a mix of control tools, logs, and live displays.
Staff react when correlator status indicates that something is wrong.
Handling of the data stream depends on operator attention and some manual intervention.
The desired system should integrate configuration, monitoring, and basic recovery into a single tied-together workflow instead of separate tasks.
The system shall reduce the amount of manual watching and intervention for routine health checks and common fault conditions.
The system shall provide a clearer real-time picture of correlator health and data flow.
Operators and scientists need sufficient visibility into observational data to trust what they are seeing while the system is running.
Alerts shall not be noisy status messages.
Automatic recovery and data processing handoff shall be treated as important capabilities that make more sense after the monitoring and alerting foundation is solid.
The dashboard shall show whether the correlator is healthy.
The dashboard shall show recent fault history for operators.
The dashboard shall support different views.
The dashboard shall avoid overwhelming scientists with low-level system noise.
Some information on the dashboard can be shared between roles.
Access to the dashboard shall be role-based.
Operators should be able to acknowledge alerts.
Operators should be able to drill into fault details.
Operators may need to pause a processing path in some cases.
Pause or resume actions should be tightly controlled.
Not every control action should be exposed on the dashboard.
The dashboard should expose only the control actions needed for day-to-day operations and incident response.
Actions that could affect the observation shall require operator approval.
Actions that could change calibration state shall require operator approval.
Actions that could risk losing data shall require operator approval.
If there is any doubt, the system shall alert first and let a person decide rather than act too aggressively.
The system shall operate the correlator as a reliable real-time part of the observatory.
The system shall support configuration of the correlator for an observation.
The system shall allow users to watch the correlator's health while data are flowing.
The system shall transform correlator output into a form that the downstream pipeline and archive can use.
The system shall keep the process visible and controllable for scientists and operators without requiring them to dig through raw engineering details.
The system shall catch faults quickly.
The system shall recover automatically when it can.
The system shall make problems obvious before they affect too much observing time.
The system shall deliver a stable data stream to storage and analysis.
Any delay or interruption in correlator operations shall be treated as causing a real cost in lost science because observatory time is extremely valuable.
The correlator operations system shall address the increased difficulty of manual monitoring and recovery caused by more demanding observing modes and larger data volumes.
The observatory shall reduce effort spent on troubleshooting so that more effort can be devoted to actual observations.
Observatory operators and scientists running observations are the primary users of the correlator operations system.
Engineers and software support staff maintain the system.
Engineers and software support staff diagnose deeper faults.
Engineers and software support staff handle updates or recovery procedures that operators should not have to do every day.
Downstream data-processing and archive teams are stakeholders.
Downstream data-processing and archive teams depend on the correlator output being well formed and timely.

The system shall present the terms "setup," "configuration," and "mode" clearly because they can mean different things depending on whether they refer to the observing intent, the correlator state, or the software configuration.
The system shall present "data quality" clearly because scientists may use it to mean the scientific result, while engineers may use it to mean signal integrity, timing, or hardware health.
The system shall not assume that all users interpret domain-specific terms in the same way.
Issues can develop too quickly or across too many channels for a person to spot them by watching screens alone, especially during busy observations.
When something goes wrong, it can be difficult to determine whether the cause is a local fault, a timing problem, or a configuration mismatch without combining several sources of information.
The monitoring system shall handle noisy alarms that occur at higher rates and with more moving parts.
Operators shall be able to distinguish real faults from expected transients and downstream processing lag.
The system shall interface with telescope control and scheduling systems to receive the observing setup and determine when an observing run starts and stops.
The audit trail shall include a timestamp.
The audit trail shall include the subsystem involved.
The audit trail shall include who or what triggered the state change.
The audit trail shall include the before-and-after state.
The system shall track configuration changes as important events.
The system shall track start and stop actions as important events.
The system shall track alarms acknowledged by an operator as important events.
The system shall track automatic restarts or failovers as important events.
The system shall track manual overrides and data-quality flags as important events.
The history shall be easy to view alongside the run summary and quality indicators.
Users shall be able to click into a specific period to see exactly what happened.
Users shall be able to review the history without digging through raw logs.
The correlator operations system shall comply with observatory-driven reliability constraints.
The correlator operations system shall maintain uptime during observing.
The correlator operations system shall comply with observatory constraints on how changes are controlled.
The correlator operations system shall fit existing observatory security and access-control practices.
The correlator operations system shall use the logging and archival conventions required by the site.
The correlator operations system shall comply with internal software engineering and operations rules that shape deployment, monitoring, and recovery.
The correlator operations system shall support secure data handling.
The correlator operations system shall enforce controlled access.
The correlator operations system shall provide traceable operations.
If the correlator operations system uses common network protocols or storage interfaces, it shall follow established interoperability practices.
The correlator operations system shall not require operators to babysit it during an observing run.
The correlator operations system shall remain available during observing runs and recover automatically from common failures.
Changes to the correlator operations system shall normally be performed through controlled maintenance windows.
Changes to the correlator operations system shall be planned with rollback in mind.
Configuration changes shall not jeopardize a live observation.
The correlator operations system shall use conservative automation.
The correlator operations system shall require clear operator approval for risky actions.
The correlator operations system shall provide strong monitoring to detect trouble early without interrupting observing unless absolutely necessary.
The audit trail shall capture enough detail to reconstruct exactly what the system was doing at any moment.
The audit trail shall capture the reason provided for an event, if one was provided.
The audit trail shall be organized as a time-ordered history tied to each observing run and configuration.
The audit trail shall provide filters for alarms.
The audit trail shall provide filters for manual changes.
The audit trail shall provide filters for recoveries.
The audit trail shall provide filters for quality-impacting events.
The audit trail shall help operators quickly get to important items.
The system shall allow users to see whether any change was controlled and expected before trusting the data.
The system shall present a simple run summary first.
The run summary shall include the current state.
The run summary shall include key health indicators.
The run summary shall include a plain-language indication of whether the data looks usable.
The system shall allow users to open a timeline for more detail.
The timeline shall show the major state changes in order.
The timeline shall show operator actions in order.
The timeline shall provide short explanations rather than raw codes or log fragments.
The system shall provide contextual hints or tooltips for unfamiliar terms.
The system shall help new users understand what changed and why without requiring prior knowledge of internal correlator jargon.
The system shall support filtering the audit trail by time range.
The system shall support filtering the audit trail by observing run.
The system shall support filtering the audit trail by subsystem.
The system shall support filtering the audit trail by event severity.
The system shall support filtering the audit trail by whether an event was manual or automatic.
The system shall allow users to jump directly to periods around alarms.
The system shall allow users to jump directly to periods around configuration changes.
The system shall allow users to jump directly to periods around data-quality flags.
The system shall provide a compact timeline for audit trail navigation.
The system shall allow users to expand a timeline segment into details.
The system shall allow engineers to move from a high-level view to the exact event record without losing context.
The system shall show a simple summary of what the system is doing right now.
The current summary shall use green/yellow/red status indicators.
The current summary shall include the current observing state.
The current summary shall include a short plain-English note about whether the data stream looks healthy.
For historical view, the system shall provide a timeline with a few clear milestones.
For historical view, the system shall provide small trend plots for key health and quality indicators.
The historical view shall help users see when something changed and whether it mattered.
The system shall explain unusual states or alarms in ordinary language.
The system shall help new users distinguish a routine transition from a real problem without digging through logs.
The system shall support keyboard-only navigation and screen readers.
The system shall provide high-contrast views.
The system shall allow adjustable text sizes.
The system shall use color choices that do not rely only on red and green.
The system shall ensure that critical alerts and status information are readable in a variety of lighting conditions.
The system shall ensure that critical alerts and status information do not assume the user is sitting at the main console.
The system shall handle routine, low-risk failures automatically.
The system shall treat transient communication drops and process restarts as examples of low-risk failures that can be handled automatically.
The system shall escalate to operators only when automatic recovery does not work quickly or when a fault could affect observation quality.
The system shall avoid repeated noisy alerts for the same underlying problem.
The system shall group related symptoms into one clear incident with a single recommended action.
The system shall keep the observing run moving unless it has real evidence that continuing would put data or hardware at risk.
For important health changes, the system shall reflect them almost immediately, within a few seconds.
The display does not need to redraw for every tiny fluctuation immediately.
The system shall smooth unstable readings and avoid chattering unless the change is meaningful.
For data quality and trending, the system may use a slower update cadence as long as it stays current enough to show whether the observation is still on track.
Maintenance and releases shall be scheduled so they do not interrupt a live observing run.
An urgent safety issue may justify interrupting a live observing run for maintenance or releases.
Updates shall go through a controlled staging and validation process before deployment.
The system shall support quick rollback if an update behaves unexpectedly.
For non-urgent changes, the system shall support planned maintenance windows.
For non-urgent changes, the system shall provide clear operator notification well in advance.
The system shall use a short confirmation delay or hysteresis for conditions that tend to flicker.
The system shall avoid alarming users over a momentary spike or a bad sample by using the confirmation delay or hysteresis.
The system shall notify immediately and without extra confirmation for conditions that suggest real damage.
The system shall notify immediately and without extra confirmation for conditions that indicate loss of data.
The system shall notify immediately and without extra confirmation for conditions that indicate a cascade failure.
The system shall balance avoiding false alarms against ensuring the operator has enough time to act before the situation worsens.
The system shall use a lower threshold for delay when the risk to the observation is higher.
The system shall provide a trend view that shows whether key metrics are improving.
The system shall provide a trend view that shows whether key metrics are stable.
The system shall provide a trend view that shows whether key metrics are degrading.
The system shall highlight the reason behind a change when possible.
The system shall help new users connect a state shift to its impact on the observation without requiring them to dig through logs.
The system shall ensure that operators can trust the information it presents during an observation.
The system shall keep routine issues from interrupting science.
The system shall provide clear, low-noise alerting.
The system shall enable users to react quickly without being buried in noise.
The system shall provide a simple dashboard showing the recent history of state changes.
The system shall provide a simple dashboard showing key health indicators in one place.
The system shall provide a simple dashboard showing key quality indicators in one place.
The system shall present short summaries of events, such as "recovered automatically" or "data quality degraded after configuration change".
The system shall present a trend chart for the most important metrics.
The system shall provide a brief explanation of what changed.
The system shall indicate whether a change affects the current scan.
Related alerts shall be grouped into a single incident when they clearly indicate the same underlying problem.
The incident shall include a short summary and a few likely next actions.
Recommended actions shall not be overly prescriptive unless the response is routine and well understood.
For serious or ambiguous cases, the incident shall identify what is affected and what to check first.
The final decision shall remain with the human operator.
The system shall label configuration changes clearly in the event timeline.
The system shall label warnings clearly in the event timeline.
The system shall label faults clearly in the event timeline.
The system shall label operator interventions clearly in the event timeline.
The system shall provide a simple trend display for data quality.
The system shall provide a short narrative summary of data quality or system changes.
The system shall allow users to click from a summary into more detail.
The default view shall answer what changed.
The default view shall answer when the change occurred.
The default view shall answer whether the observation is still usable.
The system should keep any learning from operator responses bounded and transparent.
If the system notices that operators usually handle a certain pattern the same way, it should suggest the likely recovery step next time.
If the system notices that operators usually handle a certain pattern the same way, it should group alerts more intelligently next time.
The system should save operator time and reduce repeat decision-making by using learned patterns.
The system should not fully automate actions based only on past operator behavior.
The system should account for changes in the correlator and observing conditions before reusing old patterns, because old patterns are not always safe to reuse.
The system shall clearly tie together what happened operationally, what automatic recovery it performed, and how data quality changed afterward.
The system shall provide traceability that allows users to judge quickly whether an observation is still trustworthy or needs intervention.
The system shall support operators in deciding when to step in.
The system shall help scientists understand whether a brief fault likely affected only a small portion of the data or something more serious.
The system shall display critical faults essentially immediately, within a few seconds.
The alert message shall state what failed.
The alert message shall state how serious the failure is.
The alert message shall indicate whether observing should continue.
An operator shall be able to reconstruct the last few minutes of state changes and recovery actions without digging through raw logs.
The event history timeline shall remain understandable under real observing load.
The system shall show timely indicators and trends for data quality monitoring.
The data quality monitoring display shall be understandable to a new operator without special training.
Alerting thresholds shall be tunable by operations staff.
Alert severity levels shall be tunable by operations staff.
Alert suppression rules shall be tunable by operations staff.
The system shall handle well-understood recovery steps automatically.
The system shall require explicit operator confirmation before performing any action that could affect the observation in a major or irreversible way.
The system shall treat patterns learned from past operator behavior with caution because a response that was correct in one observing mode or hardware state may be incorrect in another.
The system shall not adapt alert suppression without showing why the suppression changed.
The system shall not adapt escalation without showing why the escalation changed.
The system shall not adapt recovery actions without showing why the recovery action changed.
The system shall support a careful review process for learned behaviors.
The system shall limit how quickly learned behaviors are allowed to change.
The system shall use suggestive rather than autonomous learning.
The system shall highlight similar past incidents.
The system shall require operator approval before applying a suggested response.
The system shall adapt report prioritization based on observed patterns.
The system shall explain the basis for a suggestion.
The system shall allow operators to override suggestions easily.
The system shall treat learned behavior as mode-specific and configuration-specific rather than as a single global rule set.
When the observing mode or correlator setup changes, the system shall fall back to conservative defaults until it has enough evidence that the learned pattern still applies.
The system shall support periodic human review of learned recommendations.
The system shall provide a way to quickly disable or roll back any adaptation if it starts producing misleading alerts or recovery suggestions.
The system shall notify operators when it changes alert handling or starts suggesting a new recovery pattern.
The system shall present notifications concisely and tie them to the specific reason for the change.
The system shall support periodic review and approval for adaptations that affect escalation or suppression.
The system shall allow simple tuning of display priority to remain automatic if the tuning is reversible.
The system shall provide manual override and disable controls that are easy to find.
The system shall tie each explanation directly to the triggering evidence.
The system shall indicate whether a change was learned from local history or configured by an engineer.
The system shall indicate whether the change affects alerting.
The system shall indicate whether the change affects grouping.
The system shall indicate whether the change affects recovery advice.
The system shall include the trigger event in the notification.
The system shall include the confidence level or the amount of history supporting the change.
The system shall indicate whether the operator can immediately undo the change.
The system should require confirmation that shows the operational impact before a manual override or disable action takes effect.
The system should clearly remember and display the override status so operators can determine whether a learned rule is still active without guessing.
Operators shall set up the correlator for the planned observation.
Operators shall watch the correlator continuously while the array is running.
The system shall ensure that correlator output is transformed into usable data without gaps or corruption.
The system shall show whether the correlator is healthy during the observation run.
The system shall flag faults quickly enough for someone to act on them.
The system shall ingest correlator output in real time once the observation starts.
The system shall assemble correlator output into the correct form for storage and later analysis.
The system shall recover automatically from failures when it can.
The system shall preserve as much good data as possible when a failure occurs.
Changes to the correlator must be coordinated with the observing schedule and the current state of the array.
If a pause or restart is needed because of a fault, the system must perform it in a controlled way.
If a change is not safe, the system should hold it pending or reject it outright depending on whether it can be applied later without breaking the observation.
For the data stream, the system should continue processing only the valid portion and clearly separate any interval affected by the failed request or interruption.
The system shall protect operational status data.
The system shall be supportable by the operations staff on duty.
The system shall be maintainable as the correlator and processing chain evolve.
The system shall make it easy to add new health checks as the observatory’s needs change.
Changes to the system shall remain controlled and testable.
The system shall support incremental improvement while preserving reliability and traceability.
The initial release shall include core configuration.
The system shall support observations day to day.
The system shall support live operations reliably.
Richer analytics can wait for later phases.
More advanced visualization can wait for later phases.
Broader integrations can wait for later phases.
Specialized reports can wait for later phases.
The system shall apply a correlator change immediately if it can be made without altering the meaning or continuity of the current scan.

The system shall defer a correlator change until a safe boundary such as the end of the scan or a planned pause if the change would affect calibration, data formatting, or any live processing state in a way that could confuse downstream users.
The system shall reject a correlator change if it would clearly compromise the current observation or violate the observing plan.

The system shall determine whether to apply, defer, or reject a correlator change based on the current observing state, the type of requested change, and any known dependency on the processing pipeline.
When the system defers or rejects a correlator change request, it shall explain the reason in operational terms rather than returning a generic error.

The system shall determine whether to continue from a valid portion of disrupted data based on whether the unaffected portion still has clear scientific meaning and can be separated cleanly from the disrupted part.
If a valid segment is trustworthy on its own, the system shall continue from that point.
If the system continues from a valid segment, it shall mark the bad interval so downstream users know exactly where the break occurred.
If a disruption contaminates the whole product or makes the boundary ambiguous, the system shall stop that product rather than risk handing out misleading data.
The system shall preserve usable data when it can be isolated.
The system shall not salvage a stream if doing so would blur the line between good and bad information.
The system shall make the decision conservatively.
Approval for a data export should come from someone with operational authority for the data set.
Export approval should be based on the staff member's role and the purpose of the export.
Routine internal exports may be subject to lighter-weight approval controls.
Exports leaving the observatory or involving near-real-time products should be controlled more carefully and may require explicit approval.
The system shall allow only authorized staff to request or release exports.
The system shall allow export of the needed data product.
The system shall strip or restrict sensitive operational details when appropriate during export.
Sensitive operational details may include internal host information, security-relevant diagnostics, and unreleased observing information.
Near-real-time data shall have additional restrictions so it is not broadly redistributed until cleared for that purpose.
Users need to be able to start a scan.
Users need to be able to stop a scan.
Users need to be able to confirm that output is being assembled correctly for storage.
The system shall support setup as an important work step for correlator operations.
The system shall support live monitoring as an important work step for correlator operations.
The system shall support reacting to faults as an important work step for correlator operations.
The system shall support handing data off cleanly to the next processing stage.
The system shall support handing data off cleanly to the archive stage.
All operational terms shall be understood in the same way by everyone involved so that operations can proceed smoothly.
The system shall use the term "good data" consistently.
The system shall use the term "safe to change" consistently.
The system shall define operational boundaries for later-phase capabilities even if those capabilities are not built yet.
The system shall make rich analytics and specialized reports available only after the underlying data product is validated and no longer provisional.
The system shall limit advanced visualization when the stream is live, unstable, or partially recovered.
The system shall defer broader integrations until the core operational workflow is proven and external system visibility can be controlled.
The system shall withhold any feature that could influence active observing decisions unless it is based on trusted current state.
Later-phase features shall comply from the start with the system's rules for data quality, operational safety, and release status.
During busy periods, the system shall support more simultaneous observations.
During busy periods, the system shall operate with less tolerance for delay or backpressure.
Future observing modes should be assumed to be substantially more demanding than current observing modes.
New observing modes may increase channel count.
New observing modes may increase time resolution.
New observing modes may increase the number of simultaneous outputs.
Increases in channel count, time resolution, or simultaneous outputs will raise the processing and monitoring load.
The core operations path should have headroom for growth.
The core operations path should not be designed to fit only today's steady state.
A step change in data volume should be treated as likely rather than exceptional.
The design should avoid hard-coded limits where possible.
The design should make scaling constraints very visible.
The system shall allow rerouting around a dead path as a live change.
The system shall allow switching to a safe degraded mode as a live change.
Changes that alter calibration shall be held for a controlled window.
Changes that alter output interpretation shall be held for a controlled window.
Changes that alter the structure of the processing chain shall be held for a controlled window.
The system shall defer changes when there is doubt about whether they would affect the observation.
The system shall provide a clear distinction between recovery and reconfiguration.
Major behavioral changes shall require operator approval.
Major behavioral changes shall probably be scheduled for a planned test or maintenance period.
The system shall define the controlled-and-testable items now at least at the category level.
The system shall treat any interface that operators rely on as controlled.
Monitoring thresholds shall be controlled if changing them would alter alarms.
Data product definitions shall be controlled if changing them would alter the meaning of the output.
The exact implementation details shall remain tentative for now.
The rule that those areas are protected shall not remain tentative.
A recovery action should restore the service without corrupting the current data stream.
A recovery action should not hide the underlying fault.
A configuration change or new health check should be verified to do what it claims.
A configuration change or new health check should produce accurate alerts.
A configuration change or new health check should not create extra noise during an actual observing run.
A configuration change or new health check should not create operator confusion during an actual observing run.
Changes should be logged and traceable so the system can be reviewed afterward.
Access to operations, engineering, or validation activities should be limited to people who actually need it.
If real observatory data or restricted metadata is used, only approved users should be able to see it.
Test environments should use sanitized or representative data by default.
Real sensitive data should be used in test environments only when there is a clear operational reason.
The staging or simulation environment shall be sufficiently close to the live correlator and pipeline to exercise the same timing expectations.
The staging or simulation environment shall be sufficiently close to the live correlator and pipeline to exercise the same failure modes.
The exception to using sanitized data should be allowed only when synthetic or anonymized data is insufficient to validate the specific operational behavior being tested.
When real data is used for a test, the system should keep only the minimum amount of real data needed for the test.
When real data is used for a test, any data that is not essential to the validation goal should be sanitized.
If a field is not required to prove that a change works, it should be masked or removed.
The audit log for test environment access shall record the person or service account.
The audit log for test environment access shall record the time of access.
The audit log for test environment access shall record the environment or dataset touched.
The audit log for test environment access shall record the action taken.
The audit log for test environment access shall record the approval or ticket that authorized the access.
The audit log for test environment access shall include enough detail to reconstruct the activity later.
The audit log for test environment access shall record whether data was viewed.
The audit log for test environment access shall record whether data was copied.
The audit log for test environment access shall record whether data was modified.
The audit log for test environment access shall record whether data was used in a test run.
The audit log for test environment access shall not record the sensitive contents themselves.
The audit log shall satisfy accountability without exposing more operational information than necessary.
A live-impacting change may proceed without operations sign-off only if it is a fully automated safeguard action.
A routine self-recovery step with no change to observing intent may proceed without operations sign-off.
The system shall require operations approval for a partially reversible change if undoing it could leave gaps.
The system shall allow automation to act only when the action is bounded.
The system shall demonstrate that the correlator has re-synchronized cleanly after a disruption.
The system shall demonstrate that the pipeline has restarted from a known checkpoint or otherwise recovered in a controlled way after a disruption.
The system shall show current health indicators as green after recovery.
The system shall have configuration that matches the expected observing setup after recovery.
The system shall provide at least a short period of stable output after recovery before normal operation is declared.
For significant recovery events, the system shall undergo a brief operator review of the recovery evidence before full trust in the output resumes.
The new approach shall keep the observatory able to configure and monitor the correlator in real time.
The new approach shall keep the data stream moving into usable products.
The replacement shall preserve operations without forcing the team to relearn everything at once.
Later-phase features shall only be enabled once the core live path is stable.
Later-phase features shall only be enabled once recovery behavior has been proven.
Analytics and reporting may be enabled first if they are read-only and based on trusted output.
Visualization and external integrations shall require extra caution if they could confuse operators or feed other systems with unverified status.
Any feature that writes back shall remain unavailable until the team is confident the data stream is stable and the semantics are settled.
Any feature that automates decisions shall remain unavailable until the team is confident the data stream is stable and the semantics are settled.
Any feature that exposes operational status outside the control room shall remain unavailable until the team is confident the data stream is stable and the semantics are settled.
The system should separate general reporting from reporting that includes troubleshooting detail or performance anomalies.
A report may remain in the trusted-summary category if it shows only stable, aggregated information that has already been cleared as part of normal operations.
A trusted-summary report may include session status, uptime, and high-level performance trends.
Whether a report is acceptable depends on whether it is useful for routine oversight only.
The system shall require explicit operations approval before publishing an incident-sensitive dataset.
The system shall present the incident-sensitive dataset to the operations lead or incident owner for release approval.
Any change that can alter alarms or the meaning of output shall go through a controlled change process.
Before production use, the change shall be tested in staging or shadow mode against real or representative data.
The change shall have a clear rollback path to the previous thresholds or definition.
The rollout should be gradual if possible rather than a hard switch.
Staging or shadow testing shall be sufficient when the change is limited.
Staging or shadow testing shall be sufficient when the impact is easy to understand.
Staging or shadow testing shall be sufficient when the results match the old behavior closely enough that only sensitivity or presentation is being adjusted.
Staging or shadow testing shall be sufficient when the change does not alter the underlying operational meaning.
The change shall run cleanly through a few real observing sessions without introducing false alarms.
The change shall run cleanly through a few real observing sessions without introducing missed alarms.
The change shall run cleanly through a few real observing sessions without introducing confusion for operators.
A longer trial and more review shall be required before go-live if the change touches a critical threshold.
The change shall be blocked entirely if the new behavior cannot be validated against real conditions.
The rollout of the new behavior shall be gradual.
The rollout shall be expanded only after operators confirm the new behavior behaves as expected in real observing.
An immediate rollback to the previous trusted behavior shall be triggered if there is a spike in false alarms, missed alarms, inconsistent outputs, or operator uncertainty.
Rollback shall be mandatory if the new definition changes how a live decision would be made and the difference cannot be quickly explained or verified.
Access to real observatory data in staging or simulation shall be tightly limited to people directly involved in validating the system.
If the data includes restricted metadata or anything sensitive about live operations, approval from the operations lead or data owner shall be required before the data is used.
A developer or tester shall not be able to approve use of restricted metadata or sensitive live-operations data on their own.
Access to real observatory data in staging or simulation shall be time-limited and scoped to the specific session or test purpose.
The system shall log who requested access to real observatory data.
The staging environment should use masked or reduced datasets by default when possible.
A read-only feature shall remain disabled if its output is known to be incomplete.
Any feature that could cause someone outside the control room to act on stale or partial information shall stay off until it is safe to share.
A feature shall be held back if the data contains sensitive operational context that has not been cleared for the intended audience.
A feature shall be delayed if there is any doubt about whether the view could be mistaken for authoritative.
Staging access shall start only when there is a specific approved test or validation activity.
Staging access shall end automatically when the session is over or when the access window expires.
The system shall enforce staging access restrictions strictly so that staging does not drift into general use.

A renewal may remain under the same approval when it has the same test objective, the same people, the same dataset or environment scope, and only requires more time to complete what was already approved.
A simple extension is sufficient when the request is only a short overrun on the original session with the same purpose and the same controls.
The monitoring and output path shall have enough headroom that a normal increase in load does not push it right up against the limit during routine observing.
The design must accommodate reasonable near-term expansion without a full rewrite.
A change may be treated as an incremental extension if it can be handled by tuning thresholds, adding a parser, widening a buffer, or introducing another check without changing the basic data flow.
A change shall be treated as a redesign issue rather than a simple configuration change once it affects timing guarantees, ordering, fault handling, or the way operators interpret the data.
Any change that could compromise real-time behavior or make the monitoring less trustworthy shall undergo a more formal review before implementation.
When the system is in a provisional, recovering, or unstable state, the system shall limit any output that could be mistaken for final science-quality output or authoritative health status.
A change should be considered for formal review if it changes how people actually run or trust the system.
A change that only adds another supported case inside the existing model can remain incremental.
Access to observatory operations data shall be tightened whenever the data reveals live operational status.
Observatory operations data tied to internal troubleshooting shall be treated as restricted until it is cleared for broader use.
Routine summarized status data with no operational sensitivity may be shared more normally.
Data that includes live control commands should be automatically treated as restricted.
Access to operational data should be restricted by role so that routine observers can see summarized status.
Only operations staff can see the more detailed real-time behavior.
The exact role names and thresholds must match the site policy.
Anything exposing active control or troubleshooting should not be broadly visible.
During an incident or a formal drill, a routine observer may be allowed to see more than the usual summary if doing so helps them understand what is happening without disturbing operations.
A routine observer may be told that the system is degraded and which broad subsystem is affected.
The system shall be treated as unsafe once it can no longer absorb normal spikes without missing deadlines.
After the capacity limit is crossed, the system shall require either more capacity or a redesign of the processing path rather than accepting the extra load.
The criterion for determining when the real-time path is no longer acceptable for normal use shall be tied to sustained latency and whether recovery is falling behind, not just average throughput.
Stale alarms or outputs shall be treated as a hard stop, even if the average rate looks fine.
